The Sun Beneath the Earth

A Deep History of the Underworld, Archetypal Descent, and the Objective Psyche

🧵 

---

Images attached 

The Amduat: Ancient Egyptian Book of the Underworld

An illustrated Egyptian funerary text showing the sun god’s nightly journey through the underworld. It represents death, transformation, and the sun’s rebirth at dawn.

Amduat Papyrus Inscribed for Tiye

This papyrus depicts Tiye encountering gods and sacred beings within the Duat. It reflects the belief that ritual knowledge helped the dead travel safely through the hidden world.

The Sarcophagus of Sety I

The stone sarcophagus of Pharaoh Sety I is covered with detailed underworld scenes and religious texts. Its imagery presents the tomb as a cosmic chamber where the deceased joins the sun’s cycle of death and renewal.

---

Introduction: The Country Below Consciousness

The underworld is among the oldest and most durable constructions of the human imagination. Long before it became Hell, Hades, the Duat, Irkalla, Yomi, Xibalba, Mictlan, or any other named geography, it existed as a conjunction of elementary facts: bodies disappear into earth; daylight sinks beneath the horizon; sleepers become motionless while entering populated worlds; caves open inside apparently solid ground; blood and seed emerge from concealed interiors; memory keeps the dead active after their bodies have ceased to answer. From these facts, humanity did not infer one universal doctrine. It repeatedly built variations on a terrifying architecture: another order is present beneath the visible one, the living are not sovereign over it, and contact with it transforms whoever crosses its boundary.

The archaeological record does not preserve the first underworld myth. It preserves bodies placed in pits, ochre beside bones, chambers entered with fire, hands converted into negative images on stone, hybrid beings painted where daylight could not reach, houses constructed above ancestors, skulls removed and refashioned, tombs supplied as dwellings, and routes for the dead inscribed on gold. These remains do not speak with one voice. A burial cannot by itself demonstrate a belief in immortality. A deep cave is not automatically a temple. A composite animal-human figure is not automatically a shaman. Yet the recurrence of descent, enclosure, darkness, transformation, and return is too structurally rich to dismiss as an accident of vocabulary. The evidence demands a method capable of holding two propositions at once: no single secret tradition runs unbroken from the Paleolithic to analytical psychology, and the underworld nonetheless recurs because the human organism, human landscapes, and human institutions continually regenerate its conditions.

The underworld is therefore best understood neither as a primitive mistake nor as a merely literary theme. It is a psychic technology: a historically variable ensemble of images, spaces, bodily practices, narratives, and social roles through which a community gives form to experiences that exceed ordinary egoic control. It makes death imaginable without making death harmless. It gives grief a route, terror a geography, initiation a sequence, and psychic disintegration a possibility of return. It converts darkness into an instrument. Its rivers separate states; its gates regulate passage; its guardians personify resistance; its monsters give contour to undifferentiated dread; its judges transform guilt into procedure; its dead make memory speak; its hidden treasures represent value that cannot be obtained on the surface. The underworld is not simply where the dead go. It is where the living locate everything that remains effective after it has vanished from sight.

This essay traces that technology across deep prehistory, the earliest literate civilizations, classical and late-antique ritual worlds, medieval Christianity, alchemy, modern Spiritualism, and the psychology of C. G. Jung. Its diagnostic center is the celebrated and contested case of Emil Schwyzer, the psychiatric patient whose vision of a phallic appendage extending from the sun was compared by Jung and his associates to a wind-producing tube in the so-called Mithras Liturgy. The case matters not because it single-handedly proves a collective unconscious. It matters because it concentrates the entire problem of archetypal evidence: an embodied perceptual event becomes a cosmic image; the image resembles an ancient text unknown to the experiencer; cultural history, physiology, translation, clinical interpretation, and inherited disposition converge; and no single explanatory level exhausts the event.

At stake is the meaning of what Jung called the objective psyche. The phrase does not require the unconscious to be a supernatural country hidden under geological strata. It identifies the psyche’s capacity to produce formations that are not commanded by the conscious personality and that confront it with the force of something encountered. Dreams arrive rather than being authored line by line. Affect reorganizes perception before reflection can intervene. Complexes speak in borrowed voices. Images combine materials the ego did not knowingly assemble. Groups become possessed by figures no individual designed. The psyche is “objective” in this limited but radical sense: it is an event-field with agencies, constraints, inheritances, and emergent forms of its own.

The historical thesis is that the underworld develops wherever five conditions converge:

1. A material below: graves, caves, mines, foundations, subterranean water, darkness beneath the horizon.
2. A physiological passage: sleep, dream, trance, grief, fasting, sensory deprivation, intoxication, illness, sexual excitation, suffocation, or proximity to death.
3. A symbolic grammar: descent, gates, guides, stripping, ordeal, encounter, sacrifice, knowledge, and possible return.
4. A social apparatus: mourners, priests, mediums, initiates, rulers, healers, texts, tombs, theaters, and courts of judgment.
5. An autonomous remainder: something appears that cannot be reduced to the declared intention of those who entered the process.

The deepest claim is not that all underworlds are the same. It is that they are transformations of one recurrent human problem: consciousness is surrounded, supported, and eventually defeated by what it cannot illuminate. The sun itself becomes the supreme image of this condition. It appears sovereign only by day. Every evening it is swallowed. In the Egyptian nocturnal books, the sun does not evade the kingdom of death; it acquires the power to rise by entering it, joining with the dead god, and being regenerated in the most dangerous hour. Jung’s psychology radicalizes the same morphology. Consciousness does not become whole by remaining solar. It must discover the sun beneath the earth.

---

I. What an Underworld Is

An underworld is not defined solely by vertical location. Many traditions place the dead in the west, beyond water, inside mountains, in a shadow-double of the present world, or in an invisible order contiguous with ordinary life. The English word underworld compresses these heterogeneous arrangements into a spatial metaphor. Its value lies in the metaphor’s depth: “under” means not only beneath the feet but beneath notice, beneath speech, beneath social legitimacy, beneath the threshold of voluntary control. The underworld is whatever a culture positions on the far side of ordinary visibility while continuing to regard it as causally alive.

Four qualities recur more reliably than any map.

First, the underworld is asymmetric. Entry is easier than exit. The dead outnumber the living; the past accumulates while the present passes; descent follows gravity, whereas ascent requires labor, permission, substitution, rescue, or transformation. Myths convert the thermodynamic and political inequality between loss and recovery into geography. Inanna passes downward through seven gates, surrendering an item of power at each; Orpheus can retrieve Eurydice only under a condition he fails to sustain; Izanagi escapes Yomi but cannot reverse the corruption of death; the Maya Hero Twins return only after defeat, death, dismemberment, deception, and reconstitution. An underworld without asymmetry would be another room. Its danger consists in the fact that crossing changes the terms of agency.

Second, it is jurisdictional. The below has laws. Its rulers are often terrifying not because they are chaotic, but because they administer an order indifferent to surface preference. Ereshkigal’s realm cannot simply be violated by Inanna’s accumulated powers. Hades is not the Greek devil; he is the sovereign of an allotment from which the dead do not ordinarily return. Egyptian gates know names and require knowledge. Mictlan imposes a sequence of obstacles. Medieval Hell and Purgatory turn moral consequence into architecture. Even dream underworlds possess this quality: the dreamer may discover that wishing does not dissolve the scene. A psychic image becomes numinous when it appears to obey a law not invented by the observing ego.

Third, the underworld is conservative in the literal sense that it keeps what the surface loses. Bones, ancestors, obsolete gods, rejected affects, defeated peoples, unperformed possibilities, forgotten languages, crimes, debts, and infantile terrors collect below. This is why descent is archaeological even when no archaeology is intended. The traveler meets earlier strata of the self and of the culture. Jung’s famous house dream gives this intuition architectural form: a modern upper story opens onto older rooms, a Roman cellar, and finally a prehistoric cave containing bones and artifacts. The image is not an empirical map of the brain. It is a model of psychic temporality in which the superseded is not annihilated. It remains structural.

Fourth, the underworld is generative. The place of the dead is repeatedly also a womb, treasury, seedbed, forge, or reservoir of fertility. Crops emerge from buried seed. Ore comes from mountains and must be broken, heated, killed, and reborn as metal. Infants emerge from a hidden interior through blood. Dreams generate images while the conscious body lies inert. The sun rises from the direction in which it had vanished. This convergence does not erase the difference between tomb and womb; it gives the underworld its most disturbing charge. What destroys form also prepares form. Death is not romanticized. It is recognized as the condition in which fixed arrangements dissolve and their elements become available for another organization.

The underworld can therefore be modeled as a transformation function:

> visible identity → separation from ordinary order → reduction or dismemberment → encounter with autonomous powers → irreversible alteration → return, substitution, or captivity

The sequence is not a claim that every myth contains every stage. It is a comparative instrument. Its power lies in showing why underworld stories repeatedly become initiation stories, political stories, healing stories, and theories of artistic creation. Each concerns the destruction of an established organization and the hazardous emergence of another.

---

II. Before Myth Had Writing: Burial and the Invention of the Below

The oldest archaeological evidence relevant to an underworld is not an image of a god. It is the deliberate handling of a corpse. At Qafzeh Cave in present-day Israel, anatomically modern humans were intentionally buried roughly 100,000 years ago; the site also yielded ochre associated with the remains. The Smithsonian describes the assemblage as one of the earliest known intentional burials and notes that ochre may have participated in ritual activity ([Smithsonian Human Origins Program](https://t.co/iQv2rJCuHN)). Such evidence is momentous, but it must be read at the resolution it can bear. A grave does not reveal a complete doctrine of the soul. It does demonstrate that a corpse could be distinguished from refuse, positioned, marked, and inserted into a durable relation with place. The dead body became an object of composition.

That act creates a minimal underworld. A person who formerly moved horizontally among others is relocated vertically. The social body remains above; the physical body is entrusted to a below. Earth becomes both separator and keeper. The grave prevents immediate visual contact, yet it also fixes the dead at a known location. Burial is therefore an operation of simultaneous absence and presence. It removes the corpse while giving memory an address.

The use of red ochre intensifies this ambiguity. Across many prehistoric contexts, ochre appears in bodies, objects, surfaces, and burials. Its color can evoke blood, but no universal code can be assumed. Its durability, brilliance, tactile properties, and capacity to transform skin and stone are enough to make it a powerful medium. When applied in a mortuary context, it changes a body from something merely decomposing into something treated. The pigment is a thin mineral membrane between biological death and social form.

The dead body itself is an archetypal provocation. It is perceptually almost identical to the sleeping body and ontologically unlike it. The face remains while responsiveness has vanished. This disjunction invites a division between visible vehicle and invisible agency. Breath—present, warm, mobile, and impossible to hold—becomes an obvious candidate for life’s missing principle. Dreams then complicate the division: the dead may appear alive, speak, accuse, request, or embrace. A bereaved person can know that someone is dead and encounter that person with full affective immediacy during sleep. The earliest concepts of soul cannot be reconstructed from this fact alone, but the experiential matrix is ancient and universal enough to explain why death rarely remains a purely negative proposition.

Burial also teaches vertical memory. Each interment creates a stratum; each later generation walks over an accumulation it did not witness being made. At settlements where the dead were placed beneath houses, the floor becomes a membrane between present domestic life and ancestral presence. At Neolithic Çatalhöyük, individuals were buried beneath house platforms and floors. Whatever the precise beliefs of its inhabitants, the material arrangement refused a clean spatial exile of the dead. Domestic space rested literally on mortuary depth. The house was not merely shelter for the living. It was an occupied cross-section of time.

At Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites in the Levant, selected skulls were removed, modeled with plaster, painted, and sometimes supplied with shells for eyes. These objects should not be forced into a single “ancestor cult,” because their uses and identities varied. Yet their operation is unmistakable: decomposition is interrupted by reconstruction. The most individualized part of the body is detached from the rest, given a new surface, and returned to visibility. The dead do not simply persist. They are manufactured as social presences.

This is the first dark law of the underworld: the invisible dead require carriers. A grave, skull, mask, name, dream, statue, text, relic, photograph, or medium can become such a carrier. None is identical to the person. Each permits an absent agency to re-enter collective attention. Mortuary culture begins when biological death ceases to settle the question of social existence.

---

III. The Cave as Organ

A cave is not merely an empty space beneath rock. It is a topological contradiction: an exterior body containing an interior world. Its entrance is visible, but its depth is not. Temperature changes at the threshold. Daylight weakens. Sound detaches from visible source and returns as echo. Scale becomes uncertain. Passages constrict the body, then open abruptly into chambers. Moisture gleams. Mineral growth resembles bone, tooth, curtain, breast, or organ. The cave seems less constructed than discovered, yet to enter it is to move through an architecture whose author cannot be seen.

The cave therefore supplies the underworld with a body before theology supplies it with a name. It has a mouth, throat, chambers, secretions, and depths. It receives the dead and preserves images. It converts the human figure into a moving point of fire within enormous darkness. It can be womb, tomb, intestine, skull, or world—all without ceasing to be stone.

The history of cave art now extends far beyond the old European story centered on Lascaux and Altamira. Recent uranium-series dating in Sulawesi has pushed known representational and narrative imagery beyond fifty thousand years ([Oktaviana et al., 2024](https://t.co/jIbsojTerl)), and 2026 research reports hand stencils at least 67,800 years old ([Nature research briefing](https://t.co/ptVj7V3IJ3)). European sites remain indispensable—Chauvet's principal occupations and art reach approximately 37,000 years ago—but they are no longer the solitary origin point of image-making. The geographical expansion matters conceptually. It makes it less plausible to imagine a single local invention as the source of humanity's entire subterranean imagination. Different populations repeatedly discovered that rock interiors could become image-bearing worlds.

The images themselves resist reduction. Animals dominate many assemblages, but species frequency does not simply mirror diet. Human figures are rare, often schematic or hybridized. Hands appear as positive impressions or as absences made visible by pigment blown around them. A stencil is especially profound: the body makes an image by blocking color. The hand is present during production, absent in the final mark, and preserved as the contour of that absence. It is a Paleolithic grammar of the ghost.

The deep placement of some art adds another dimension. Images located far from entrances required fuel, preparation, orientation, and risk. Flickering flame would animate contours differently from museum illumination. Reliefs in the rock could emerge and disappear as the light moved. The observer did not stand before a stable, evenly lit panel. Image, wall, flame, smoke, sound, and moving body formed one event. The animal was neither simply “on” the wall nor wholly imagined apart from it. It appeared at the unstable interface between mineral affordance and guided perception.

David Lewis-Williams and Jean Clottes famously proposed that some Upper Paleolithic cave art can be interpreted in relation to altered states of consciousness and shamanic practices. Their model, drawing partly on recurrent geometric forms in altered vision and on ethnographic analogy, has been influential and contested. The controversy is valuable. It marks the difference between recognizing a cave as a technology of consciousness and claiming to know the exact religion of its makers. “Shamanism” cannot serve as a universal solvent poured over every hybrid figure, handprint, or narrow passage. But neither should caution flatten the sensory extremity of deliberate subterranean entry.

Yafit Kedar, Gil Kedar, and Ran Barkai have added a physiological hypothesis. Their experimental modeling suggests that torches in poorly ventilated deep caves can reduce oxygen concentrations enough to contribute to hypoxia, with possible alterations in perception and bodily experience ([Kedar, Kedar, and Barkai, 2021](https://t.co/hAG8qoydJh)). The authors propose that the transformative environment of the cave may have been sought rather than accidentally endured. The hypothesis is not a demonstrated explanation of Paleolithic art as a whole. Cave geometries, ventilation, group size, fuel, duration, and individual susceptibility vary. Its importance is more exact: it restores air to the archaeology of images. The cave does not act only through symbols. It acts on the breathing body.

Darkness, acoustic reverberation, restricted posture, fatigue, fear, flame, smoke, and possibly hypoxia can shift the relation between expectation and sensation. Under ordinary daylight, perception suppresses ambiguity quickly. In deep darkness, ambiguous input persists. The nervous system must complete forms from less information. Rock becomes especially available for animation. A contour can become an animal because the environment prevents one interpretation from stabilizing permanently. The cave is thus not a neutral container in which a preexisting mythology is displayed. It is an apparatus capable of producing the experiential authority that mythology later describes.

The earliest underworld may not have been believed before it was entered. It may have been learned as a phase change of perception:

> daylight body + threshold + sensory reduction + unstable image + social expectation = inhabited depth

This formulation does not make the inhabitants unreal. It identifies the conditions under which an image ceases to feel like a voluntary picture and begins to behave like an encountered presence.

---

IV. The Dead Beneath the House

The Neolithic transformation of subsistence and settlement altered the underworld by making place itself ancestral. Mobile communities also possessed burial landscapes and deep memory, but permanent or recurrent architecture enabled a new density of vertical relation. Floors were rebuilt. Houses accumulated phases. Walls enclosed repeated births, meals, illnesses, and deaths. The same location could hold several human generations not only in memory but in sediment.

At Çatalhöyük, burial beneath platforms placed the dead within the daily geometry of the house. At Jericho and other Levantine sites, modeled skulls brought selected dead back above ground in altered form. At megalithic tombs across parts of Neolithic Europe, communal deposition created chambers that could be reopened, rearranged, and revisited. These practices differ radically, but they share a refusal to treat the dead as a closed past. The dead become part of architecture, and architecture becomes a machine for controlling return.

Control is crucial. The underworld is never only a hope that the dead survive. It is also a defense against their indiscriminate presence. A proper grave, sealed tomb, funerary offering, name, lament, or periodic rite can establish terms. The living feed, remember, invoke, appease, or exclude. The dead acquire rights and limitations. Ritual is the diplomacy of an impossible border.

This border has political consequences. Those who control tombs, genealogies, relics, and ancestral speech can claim authority over time. A ruler is stronger if the dead legitimate him. A lineage becomes territorial when ancestors are embedded in land. A priesthood gains power when it alone knows the routes, names, offerings, and purifications required for passage. Once an underworld is institutionally organized, death ceases to be only a biological event. It becomes a jurisdiction with experts.

The history of the underworld is therefore inseparable from the history of mediation. The cave specialist, mourner, embalmer, lamenter, dream interpreter, necromancer, psychopomp, priest, poet, initiate, alchemist, analyst, and medium occupy different worlds, but each stands at a threshold where an invisible order must be given a controlled form. Their authority is always unstable. If nothing appears, mediation seems empty. If too much appears, the mediator risks possession, fraud, madness, pollution, or death. The ideal operator must open the boundary without abolishing it.

This structure will persist for millennia. The medium must be permeable and bounded. The initiate must die symbolically without becoming irretrievable. The king must descend without surrendering sovereignty. The analyst must permit autonomous images without treating every image as command. The sun must enter night without becoming night forever.
